_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss in another section (Ingrid's partner vs Tariq's shared cooking; Kofi's nutritionist vs Saoirse's doubters). Used by the Part 7 practice page.
title: Fuel for the finish line
subtitle: Four athletes describe how they train and what they eat.

sections.A: Kofi, 24, sprinter. People think sprinting is just running fast for ten seconds, but my week is mostly weights, starts and very short, very painful repeats on the track, twice a day, six days a week. For years I thought I was eating well: chicken, eggs, fish, mountains of protein. Then a sports nutritionist looked at my food diary and told me I was running on empty. I simply wasn't getting enough carbohydrate to recover between sessions. Adding rice, oats and pasta made a difference within a month, and I stopped feeling so flat in the afternoons. I'm strict most of the time, but every Sunday I go to my mum's for jollof rice and fried plantain, and I eat until I can't move. My coach pretends not to know. I also sleep nine hours a night, which my friends find hilarious.
sections.B: Ingrid, 31, open-water swimmer. I swim long distances in the sea, so most mornings I'm in the water at five, whatever the weather. In March the sea round here is about eight degrees, the waves can be brutal, and some days I can't feel my feet for an hour afterwards. To cope with the distance and the cold I need around five thousand calories a day, which sounds like a dream but honestly isn't. Eating becomes a second job. I'm chewing something almost every hour, even when I'm not remotely hungry, and I get very bored of porridge. I'd never manage without my partner, Lars, who does all the shopping and cooking and prepares a huge bag of sandwiches for me to take to the beach. He jokes that he's the real athlete in the family, and on some days he may be right.
sections.C: Tariq, 19, rower. I row in the lightweight category, which means I have to be under a strict weight on race day, so I keep a very close eye on the scales and weigh most of what I eat. It can be stressful, especially near a competition. Training is on the river at six, then the gym in the evening. Last year I tried to do too much, ignored a sore back and ended up unable to row for two months. That taught me that rest days aren't lazy; they're when your body actually gets stronger. Now I take them seriously. I'm at university, and I share a house with four other rowers. On Sundays we cook together, giant pots of chilli and curry, and freeze them in portions for the week. Everyone takes a turn at chopping, though nobody trusts me with the spices.
sections.D: Saoirse, 27, track cyclist. Three years ago I stopped eating meat and fish, and several people in my club were convinced it would ruin my career. They said I'd be weak and permanently tired. Instead, that season I set two personal bests and won my first national medal, and a couple of the people who doubted me have since asked for my recipes. I get my protein from lentils, beans, tofu and nuts, and I love experimenting in the kitchen. A lot of my training happens indoors on a bike fixed to a frame, sometimes for three hours at a time, which would be unbearably dull if I didn't watch films while I pedal. I've worked through most of the detective series ever made. Track racing is as much about your head as your legs, so I also see a sports psychologist once a month.

questions.question: Which person must keep their weight under a certain limit to compete?
questions.why: 'I have to be under a strict weight on race day.'

questions.question: Which person was advised by an expert to eat more of a particular kind of food?
questions.why: A nutritionist said 'I simply wasn't getting enough carbohydrate.' Saoirse was given opinions by club members, not an expert.

questions.question: Which person finds the quantity of food they need to eat tiresome?
questions.why: Five thousand calories 'sounds like a dream but honestly isn't. Eating becomes a second job.'

questions.question: Which person showed that others were wrong about the way they eat?
questions.why: People thought giving up meat 'would ruin my career'; instead she 'set two personal bests'.

questions.question: Which person allows themselves a weekly treat?
questions.why: 'Every Sunday I go to my mum's for jollof rice… and I eat until I can't move.' Tariq's Sunday cooking is meal preparation, not a treat.

questions.question: Which person depends on someone else to make their meals?
questions.why: Lars 'does all the shopping and cooking'. Tariq shares the cooking with housemates and does his own part.

questions.question: Which person learned the value of recovery after getting injured?
questions.why: After ignoring a sore back, 'rest days aren't lazy; they're when your body actually gets stronger'. Kofi talks about recovery too, but in connection with food, not injury.

questions.question: Which person keeps themselves entertained during long training sessions?
questions.why: Indoor sessions 'would be unbearably dull if I didn't watch films while I pedal'.

questions.question: Which person trains in difficult natural conditions?
questions.why: 'In March the sea… is about eight degrees, the waves can be brutal.'

questions.question: Which person prepares food together with teammates?
questions.why: 'On Sundays we cook together… and freeze them in portions for the week.'
